claim: C. elegans larvae exhibit abrupt switching between two distinct behavioral states outside of lethargus: active wakefulness and quiet wakefulness.
source: We found that, outside of lethargus, animals exhibited abrupt switching between two distinct behavioral states: active wakefulness and quiet wakefulness.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 2C-D and 3.

claim: The durations of epochs of active wakefulness exhibited non-Poisson statistics.
source: The durations of epochs of active wakefulness exhibited non-Poisson statistics.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A, where power-law distribution was favored over exponential distribution.

claim: Increased Gαs signaling stabilized the active wakefulness state before, during and after lethargus.
source: Increased Gαs signaling stabilized the active wakefulness state before, during and after lethargus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from kin-2 and acy-1(gf) mutants shown in Figures 4 and 7-8.

claim: Decreased Gαs signaling destabilized active wakefulness outside of, but not during, lethargus.
source: In contrast, decreased Gαs signaling, decreased neuropeptide release, or decreased CREB activity destabilized active wakefulness outside of, but not during, lethargus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from acy-1(lf) mutants shown in Figures 5 and 7-8.

claim: Decreased neuropeptide release destabilized active wakefulness outside of, but not during, lethargus.
source: In contrast, decreased Gαs signaling, decreased neuropeptide release, or decreased CREB activity destabilized active wakefulness outside of, but not during, lethargus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from unc-31 mutants shown in Figures 6 and 7-8.

claim: Decreased CREB activity destabilized active wakefulness outside of, but not during, lethargus.
source: In contrast, decreased Gαs signaling, decreased neuropeptide release, or decreased CREB activity destabilized active wakefulness outside of, but not during, lethargus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from crh-1 mutants shown in Figures 6 and 7-8.

claim: Protein kinase A (PKA) stabilizes active wakefulness at least in part through neuropeptide release and CREB.
source: Taken together, our findings support a model in which protein kinase A (PKA) stabilizes active wakefulness, at least in part through two of its downstream targets: neuropeptide release and CREB.
evidence: This model is inferred from the combined experimental results of multiple mutants affecting the PKA pathway.

claim: During lethargus, when active wakefulness is strongly suppressed, the native role of PKA signaling in modulating locomotion and quiescence may be minor.
source: However, during lethargus, when active wakefulness is strongly suppressed, the native role of PKA signaling in modulating locomotion and quiescence may be minor.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that decreased Gαs signaling did not affect behavior during lethargus, as shown in Figures 5-8.

claim: Each larval stage of C. elegans lasts 8-12 hr at 20°C under standard conditions.
source: Each larval stage lasts 8–12 hr at 20°C, and under standard conditions, and ends with a molt, when epidermal cells synthesize a new cuticle and the old one is shed.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: Each molt in C. elegans is accompanied by a 2-3 hr period of behavioral quiescence called lethargus.
source: Although C. elegans larvae are mostly continuously motile, each molt is accompanied by a 2–3 hr period of behavioral quiescence (Singh and Sulston, 1978), referred to as 'lethargus'.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Singh and Sulston, 1978.

claim: C. elegans move directionally by propagating dorsoventral undulations along their body.
source: C. elegans move directionally by propagating dorsoventral undulations along their body.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans locomotion.

claim: Motoneurons provide output to longitudinal body-wall muscles to propagate body bends upon receiving input from interneurons.
source: Upon receiving input from interneurons, motoneurons provide output to an array of longitudinal body-wall muscles in order to propagate body bends (White et al., 1986; Stetina et al., 2006; Karbowski et al., 2006; Stephens et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Head/neck motoneurons and muscles independently control head movements, such as exploratory head swings.
source: Head/neck motoneurons and muscles independently control head movements, such as exploratory head swings (White et al., 1986; Stetina et al., 2006; Pirri et al., 2009; Maguire et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The gsa-1 gene encodes a Gαs subunit which activates the adenylyl cyclase ACY-1.
source: The gsa-1 gene encodes a Gαs subunit, which activates the adenylyl cyclase ACY-1, and the GSA-1(Gαs) pathway has been previously shown to affect locomotion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular pathway.

claim: Activation of ACY-1 by GSA-1 leads to the production of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP).
source: Activation ACY-1 by GSA-1 leads to the production of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular pathway.

claim: The binding of cAMP to the protein kinase A (PKA) regulatory subunit KIN-2 dissociates it from the inactive holoenzyme, releasing the PKA catalytic subunit KIN-1.
source: The binding of cAMP to the protein kinase A (PKA) regulatory subunit KIN-2 dissociates it from the inactive holoenzyme, releasing the PKA catalytic subunit, KIN-1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PKA activation.

claim: Increased PKA activity enhances signaling at the neuromuscular junction in C. elegans.
source: Increased PKA activity enhances signaling at the neuromuscular junction, as well as increases cAMP response element (CRE) mediated transcription in C. elegans neurons (Kimura et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kimura et al., 2002.

claim: Increased PKA activity increases cAMP response element (CRE) mediated transcription in C. elegans neurons.
source: Increased PKA activity enhances signaling at the neuromuscular junction, as well as increases cAMP response element (CRE) mediated transcription in C. elegans neurons (Kimura et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kimura et al., 2002.

claim: Upregulating the Gαs signaling pathway results in hyperkinetic phenotypes, typically described as a nonspecific increase in the rate of locomotion.
source: Thus, upregulating this signaling pathway has been reported to result in hyperkinetic phenotypes, typically described as a nonspecific increase in the rate of locomotion (Schade et al., 2005; Reynolds et al., 2005; Raizen et al., 2008; Perez-Mansilla and Nurrish, 2009), as well as in reduced quiescence during lethargus (Raizen et al., 2008; Belfer and Raizen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Upregulating the Gαs signaling pathway results in reduced quiescence during lethargus.
source: Thus, upregulating this signaling pathway has been reported to result in hyperkinetic phenotypes, typically described as a nonspecific increase in the rate of locomotion (Schade et al., 2005; Reynolds et al., 2005; Raizen et al., 2008; Perez-Mansilla and Nurrish, 2009), as well as in reduced quiescence during lethargus (Raizen et al., 2008; Belfer and Raizen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: PyCelegans is a high-speed, modular image-processing tool for analyzing posture and locomotion of C. elegans on high performance computing resources.
source: To assay the modulation of behavior during development, we developed PyCelegans: a high-speed, modular image-processing tool for analyzing posture and locomotion of C. elegans on high performance computing resources.
evidence: This describes the computational tool developed for the study.

claim: Using 256 cores, PyCelegans achieved a speed-up of two orders of magnitude relative to previous implementations.
source: Using PyCelegans, the rate-limiting component of the analysis scaled linearly with the number of available processing-cores. By using 256 cores we achieved a speed-up of two orders of magnitude relative to previous implementations.
evidence: This is a direct measurement of computational performance.

claim: A 2% growth of body-length per hour was observed outside of lethargus.
source: For instance, a 2% growth of body-length per hour was observed outside of lethargus, but during lethargus a 5% shortening of the body-length was observed (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: During lethargus, a 5% shortening of the body-length was observed.
source: For instance, a 2% growth of body-length per hour was observed outside of lethargus, but during lethargus a 5% shortening of the body-length was observed (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The shortening of body length during lethargus may be due to continuous growth in body-volume at a period where adding surface area to the old cuticle was restricted.
source: This shortening may be due to continuous growth in body-volume at a period where adding surface area to the (old) cuticle was restricted.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed body shortening.

claim: Body-segments that are further removed from the head of the animal exhibit more quiescence than more anterior segments.
source: Body-segments that are further removed from the head of the animal exhibit more quiescence than more anterior segments, such that the overall quiescent behavior associated with L4 lethargus reflects the quiescence of the head and the neck.
evidence: This is observed from the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The overall quiescent behavior associated with L4 lethargus reflects the quiescence of the head and the neck.
source: Body-segments that are further removed from the head of the animal exhibit more quiescence than more anterior segments, such that the overall quiescent behavior associated with L4 lethargus reflects the quiescence of the head and the neck.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that anterior segments are least quiescent and determine whole-animal behavior.

claim: The most anterior region of C. elegans was the least quiescent throughout the measurement period from mid L4int to mid young adult stage.
source: Interestingly, the most anterior region was the least quiescent throughout the measurement.
evidence: This is observed from the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mid-body region of C. elegans was the most quiescent during the measurement period from mid L4int to mid young adult stage.
source: Subsequent regions exhibited successively increasing quiescence, with the mid-body being the most quiescent.
evidence: This is observed from the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The temporal dynamics of quiescence of the entire animal mirrored that of the head/neck region.
source: As a result of this ordering, the temporal dynamics of quiescence of the entire animal mirrored that of the head/neck region.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the head/neck region is least quiescent and determines whole-animal behavior.

claim: The activity of the head/neck motoneuron circuits determined the outcome of whole-animal quiescence measurements.
source: We thus concluded that the activity of the head/neck motoneuron circuits determined the outcome of previously reported measurements of whole-animal quiescence (Raizen et al., 2008; Singh et al., 2011; Bringmann, 2011; Iwanir et al., 2013; Belfer and Raizen, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that head/neck region dynamics mirror whole-animal quiescence, combined with citations to previous work.

claim: A decrease in the percentage of time spent in forward locomotion was observed during the 4 hr preceding L4leth.
source: Aligning behavioral data by the onset of lethargus for each 10 hr measurement and averaging between animals, we observed a decrease in the percentage of time spent in forward locomotion during the 4 hr preceding L4leth and a corresponding increase in the percentage of time spent in dwelling (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed from averaged behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A corresponding increase in the percentage of time spent in dwelling was observed during the 4 hr preceding L4leth.
source: Aligning behavioral data by the onset of lethargus for each 10 hr measurement and averaging between animals, we observed a decrease in the percentage of time spent in forward locomotion during the 4 hr preceding L4leth and a corresponding increase in the percentage of time spent in dwelling (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed from averaged behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: During the first 1-2 hr following L4leth termination, wild-type behavior was characterized by a high, decreasing fraction of dwelling and a low, increasing fraction of forward locomotion.
source: During the first 1–2 hr following L4leth termination, wild-type behavior was characterized by a high, decreasing fraction of dwelling, and a low, increasing fraction of forward locomotion.
evidence: This is observed from averaged behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Backward locomotion was modulated more weakly during the measurement period from mid L4int to mid young adult stage.
source: Backward locomotion was modulated more weakly during the period of the measurement.
evidence: This is observed from averaged behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The overall curvature was modulated during lethargus.
source: In agreement with our previous findings using complementary methods (Iwanir et al., 2013) we found that the overall curvature, quantified as the mean absolute angle, was modulated during lethargus, and that the overall growth rate of the body length outside of lethargus was 2% per hour (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is observed from data shown in Figure 1D and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The propagation velocity of anterior-to-posterior body-bends was gradually downregulated during late L4int and upregulated during the early young adult stage.
source: In addition, the propagation velocity of anterior-to-posterior body-bends and the frequency of generation of bends were gradually downregulated during late L4int, and upregulated during the early young adult stage (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed from data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The frequency of generation of body-bends was gradually downregulated during late L4int and upregulated during the early young adult stage.
source: In addition, the propagation velocity of anterior-to-posterior body-bends and the frequency of generation of bends were gradually downregulated during late L4int, and upregulated during the early young adult stage (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed from data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The frequency of bend generation can serve as an adequate proxy for bend velocity throughout the measurement period.
source: The similarity between the dynamics of bend generation frequency and of bend velocity suggested that the former could serve as an adequate proxy for the latter throughout the measurement period.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed similarity between the two measurements.

claim: Active wakefulness is characterized by a high proportion of forward locomotion.
source: We found that the forward velocities of individual animals decreased gradually (data not shown). In contrast, the fraction of time spent in forward locomotion and dwelling alternated between high and low values, giving rise to the definition of two behavioral states: active wakefulness, characterized by a high proportion of forward locomotion, and quiet wakefulness, characterized by a high proportion of dwelling (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is the definition of active wakefulness based on observed behavioral patterns.

claim: Quiet wakefulness is characterized by a high proportion of dwelling.
source: We found that the forward velocities of individual animals decreased gradually (data not shown). In contrast, the fraction of time spent in forward locomotion and dwelling alternated between high and low values, giving rise to the definition of two behavioral states: active wakefulness, characterized by a high proportion of forward locomotion, and quiet wakefulness, characterized by a high proportion of dwelling (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is the definition of quiet wakefulness based on observed behavioral patterns.

claim: Transitions between active and quiet wakefulness were in the form of rapid behavioral switches.
source: Transitions between active and quiet wakefulness were in the form of rapid behavioral switches, suggesting that they represented two distinct behavioral states.
evidence: This is observed from individual animal traces shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The power law fit for epoch durations was strongly favored over the exponential fit with an Akaike weight of 0.9997.
source: Interestingly, the power law fit (Figure 3A, AIC = −3.1) was strongly favored over the exponential fit (AIC = 13.1): the Akaike weight was 0.9997, indicating that the probability that the power-law model better described the data was 99.97%.
evidence: This is the result of statistical analysis comparing two models.

claim: The exponent obtained from the power law fit of epoch durations was −(1+α) = −1.83 ± 0.31.
source: The exponent obtained from the power law fit was −(1+α) = −1.83 ± 0.31 (95% confidence intervals, R = 0.95).
evidence: This is the result of statistical fitting to the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A simple, Poissonian, model would not adequately describe the observed transitions between active and quiet wakefulness.
source: These results indicated that a simple, Poissonian, model would not adequately describe the observed transitions between active and quiet wakefulness.
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical analysis showing power-law distribution is favored over exponential.

claim: The long tail of the power-law distribution suggested that the active wakefulness state was stabilized during L4int.
source: Rather, the long tail of the power-law distribution suggested that the active wakefulness state was stabilized during L4int.
evidence: This is inferred from the power-law distribution of epoch durations.

claim: The time-averaged mean squared displacement (TMSD) exhibited power-law growth with the exponent (1−α) = 0.32 ± 0.03.
source: As shown in Figure 3C, the resulting long-term behavior was characterized by the exponent 1−α = 0.32 ± 0.03 (95% confidence intervals, R = 0.96), consistent with a value of α ≈ 0.7.
evidence: This is the result of statistical analysis of TMSD data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The loss of function mutation of the kin-2 gene results in increased activity of the PKA holoenzyme.
source: Both the loss of function mutation of the kin-2 gene—encoding a negative regulatory subunit of the cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) KIN-1—and the gain of function mutation of the adenylyl cyclase gene acy-1 were inferred to result in increased activity of the holoenzyme (Schade et al., 2005; Reynolds et al., 2005; Charlie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The gain of function mutation of the adenylyl cyclase gene acy-1 results in increased activity of the PKA holoenzyme.
source: Both the loss of function mutation of the kin-2 gene—encoding a negative regulatory subunit of the cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) KIN-1—and the gain of function mutation of the adenylyl cyclase gene acy-1 were inferred to result in increased activity of the holoenzyme (Schade et al., 2005; Reynolds et al., 2005; Charlie et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both kin-2 and acy-1(gf) mutations result in hyperkinetic behavior outside of lethargus.
source: Correspondingly, both mutations result in hyperkinetic behavior outside of lethargus and reduced quiescence during lethargus (Schade et al., 2005; Reynolds et al., 2005; Charlie et al., 2006; Perez-Mansilla and Nurrish, 2009; Belfer and Raizen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both kin-2 and acy-1(gf) mutations result in reduced quiescence during lethargus.
source: Correspondingly, both mutations result in hyperkinetic behavior outside of lethargus and reduced quiescence during lethargus (Schade et al., 2005; Reynolds et al., 2005; Charlie et al., 2006; Perez-Mansilla and Nurrish, 2009; Belfer and Raizen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In kin-2 and acy-1(gf) mutants, active wakefulness persisted from mid L4int until the onset of L4leth and resumed at the end of L4leth.
source: We found that in both cases active wakefulness persisted from mid L4int until the onset of L4leth, and resumed at the end of L4leth (Figure 4A–B,D–E).
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: kin-2 and acy-1(gf) mutants spent a significantly reduced amount of time in quiet wakefulness before and after lethargus as compared to wild-type.
source: Correspondingly, as compared to wild-type, these mutants spent a significantly reduced amount of time in quiet wakefulness before and after lethargus (Figures 4 and 7), and exhibited an approximately two-fold increase in peak velocity during L4int and milder downregulation of velocity in anticipation of L4leth (Figure 4C,F).
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: kin-2 and acy-1(gf) mutants exhibited an approximately two-fold increase in peak velocity during L4int.
source: Correspondingly, as compared to wild-type, these mutants spent a significantly reduced amount of time in quiet wakefulness before and after lethargus (Figures 4 and 7), and exhibited an approximately two-fold increase in peak velocity during L4int and milder downregulation of velocity in anticipation of L4leth (Figure 4C,F).
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 4C,F.

claim: kin-2 and acy-1(gf) mutants exhibited milder downregulation of velocity in anticipation of L4leth.
source: Correspondingly, as compared to wild-type, these mutants spent a significantly reduced amount of time in quiet wakefulness before and after lethargus (Figures 4 and 7), and exhibited an approximately two-fold increase in peak velocity during L4int and milder downregulation of velocity in anticipation of L4leth (Figure 4C,F).
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 4C,F.

claim: During bouts of non-quiescent behavior in lethargus, kin-2 and acy-1(gf) mutants exhibited a large increase in the prevalence of forward locomotion.
source: In addition, consistent with previous reports (Belfer and Raizen, 2013), during bouts of non-quiescent behavior in lethargus ('motion bouts') we observed a large increase in the prevalence of forward locomotion in kin-2 and acy-1(gf) mutants.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data and consistent with previous reports.

claim: Increased PKA activity stabilizes active wakefulness.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that increased PKA activity stabilizes active wakefulness.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of kin-2 and acy-1(gf) mutant experiments.

claim: Animals carrying a null mutation of kin-1 die as embryos.
source: Animals carrying a null mutation of kin-1 or acy-1 die as embryos or first stage larvae respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these mutants.

claim: Animals carrying a null mutation of acy-1 die as first stage larvae.
source: Animals carrying a null mutation of kin-1 or acy-1 die as embryos or first stage larvae respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these mutants.

claim: Animals carrying a partial loss of function allele of the acy-1 gene appear superficially wild-type.
source: However, animals carrying a partial loss of function allele of the acy-1 gene appear superficially wild-type.
evidence: This is an observation about the mutant phenotype.

claim: During the last 4 hr of L4int, acy-1(lf) mutants exhibited significantly exaggerated quiet wakefulness.
source: During the last 4 hr of L4int quiet wakefulness was significantly exaggerated and the active wakefulness state was fragmented—animals displayed a larger number of switches out of brief epochs of active wakefulness (Figure 5).
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: During the last 4 hr of L4int, acy-1(lf) mutants exhibited a fragmented active wakefulness state with a larger number of switches out of brief epochs.
source: During the last 4 hr of L4int quiet wakefulness was significantly exaggerated and the active wakefulness state was fragmented—animals displayed a larger number of switches out of brief epochs of active wakefulness (Figure 5).
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: After the termination of L4leth, acy-1(lf) mutants exhibited exaggerated quiet wakefulness and reduced active wakefulness.
source: Similarly, after the termination of L4leth, quiet wakefulness was exaggerated and active wakefulness was reduced.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: During L4leth, the dynamics of quiescence and locomotion of acy-1(lf) mutants were similar to wild-type.
source: However, during L4leth the dynamics of quiescence and locomotion of the mutants were similar to wild-type (Figures 7 and 8).
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: PKA activity stabilizes the active wakefulness state.
source: These results are consistent with the idea that PKA activity stabilizes the active wakefulness state.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of acy-1(lf) mutant experiments.

claim: Tomosyn is a target of PKA.
source: Tomosyn, a target of PKA (Baba et al., 2005), was shown to negatively regulate both unc-13-dependent synaptic transmitter release and unc-31-dependent neuropeptide release in C. elegans (Gracheva et al., 2006; Gracheva et al., 2007a, 2007b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baba et al., 2005.

claim: Tomosyn negatively regulates unc-13-dependent synaptic transmitter release in C. elegans.
source: Tomosyn, a target of PKA (Baba et al., 2005), was shown to negatively regulate both unc-13-dependent synaptic transmitter release and unc-31-dependent neuropeptide release in C. elegans (Gracheva et al., 2006; Gracheva et al., 2007a, 2007b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gracheva et al., 2006, 2007a, 2007b.

claim: Tomosyn negatively regulates unc-31-dependent neuropeptide release in C. elegans.
source: Tomosyn, a target of PKA (Baba et al., 2005), was shown to negatively regulate both unc-13-dependent synaptic transmitter release and unc-31-dependent neuropeptide release in C. elegans (Gracheva et al., 2006; Gracheva et al., 2007a, 2007b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gracheva et al., 2006, 2007a, 2007b.

claim: Hyper-activation of PKA can bypass the requirement for UNC-31 in the docking of dense core vesicles (DCVs).
source: Since hyper-activation of PKA could bypass the requirement for UNC-31 in the docking of dense core vesicles (DCVs), the GSA-1(Gαs) and the UNC-31/CAPS pathways were suggested to converge to control DCV release (Schade et al., 2005; Reynolds et al., 2005; Charlie et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2007; Perez-Mansilla and Nurrish, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The GSA-1(Gαs) and the UNC-31/CAPS pathways converge to control DCV release.
source: Since hyper-activation of PKA could bypass the requirement for UNC-31 in the docking of dense core vesicles (DCVs), the GSA-1(Gαs) and the UNC-31/CAPS pathways were suggested to converge to control DCV release (Schade et al., 2005; Reynolds et al., 2005; Charlie et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2007; Perez-Mansilla and Nurrish, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Outside of lethargus, unc-31 mutants exhibited increased occupation of the quiet wakefulness state.
source: As compared to wild-type animals, outside of lethargus unc-31 mutants exhibited increased occupation of the quiet wakefulness state, a fragmented active wakefulness state, and overall lower velocities.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Outside of lethargus, unc-31 mutants exhibited a fragmented active wakefulness state.
source: As compared to wild-type animals, outside of lethargus unc-31 mutants exhibited increased occupation of the quiet wakefulness state, a fragmented active wakefulness state, and overall lower velocities.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Outside of lethargus, unc-31 mutants exhibited overall lower velocities.
source: As compared to wild-type animals, outside of lethargus unc-31 mutants exhibited increased occupation of the quiet wakefulness state, a fragmented active wakefulness state, and overall lower velocities.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: During L4leth, the dynamics of quiescence and locomotion of unc-31 mutants were similar to wild-type.
source: In contrast, during L4leth, the dynamics of quiescence and locomotion of unc-31 mutants were similar to wild-type.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figures 6, 7, and 8.

claim: The mutation in the unc-31 gene resulted in elevated levels of backward locomotion outside of lethargus.
source: Unlike acy-1(lf) mutants, the mutation in the unc-31 gene resulted in elevated levels of backward locomotion outside of lethargus and a decrease in directed locomotion during motion bouts in lethargus (Figures 7 and 8).
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The mutation in the unc-31 gene resulted in a decrease in directed locomotion during motion bouts in lethargus.
source: Unlike acy-1(lf) mutants, the mutation in the unc-31 gene resulted in elevated levels of backward locomotion outside of lethargus and a decrease in directed locomotion during motion bouts in lethargus (Figures 7 and 8).
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: PKA activity stabilizes active wakefulness during L4int at least in part by regulating DCV exocytosis.
source: Taken together with the acy-1(lf) phenotype, these results support a model in which PKA activity stabilizes active wakefulness during L4int (at least in part) by regulating DCV exocytosis, but only plays a minor role in regulating locomotion during lethargus.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of acy-1(lf) and unc-31 mutant experiments.

claim: PKA only plays a minor role in regulating locomotion during lethargus.
source: Taken together with the acy-1(lf) phenotype, these results support a model in which PKA activity stabilizes active wakefulness during L4int (at least in part) by regulating DCV exocytosis, but only plays a minor role in regulating locomotion during lethargus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that acy-1(lf) and unc-31 mutants show wild-type-like behavior during lethargus.

claim: CREB is a transcription factor that induces gene expression through promoters containing the cAMP-response element (CRE) enhancer after phosphorylation by PKA.
source: Another major target of PKA is the cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB), a transcription factor that, after phosphorylation by PKA, induces gene expression through promoters containing the cAMP-response element (CRE) enhancer (Mayr and Montminy, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Mayr and Montminy, 2001.

claim: The C. elegans ortholog of CREB is CRH-1.
source: Although the C. elegans ortholog of CREB, CRH-1, was primarily implicated in long-term habituation and memory (Kimura et al., 2002; Kauffman et al., 2010; Nishida et al., 2011; Timbers and Rankin, 2011) it was possible that it could also have a role in regulating larval locomotion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the C. elegans gene.

claim: CRH-1 was primarily implicated in long-term habituation and memory.
source: Although the C. elegans ortholog of CREB, CRH-1, was primarily implicated in long-term habituation and memory (Kimura et al., 2002; Kauffman et al., 2010; Nishida et al., 2011; Timbers and Rankin, 2011) it was possible that it could also have a role in regulating larval locomotion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Outside of lethargus, crh-1 mutants exhibited more poorly-defined global locomotion states.
source: Outside of lethargus, crh-1 mutants exhibited more poorly-defined global locomotion states, although a clear active wakefulness state was observed in 4 out of 16 animals 5–6 hr prior to L4leth.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: A clear active wakefulness state was observed in 4 out of 16 crh-1 mutant animals 5-6 hr prior to L4leth.
source: Outside of lethargus, crh-1 mutants exhibited more poorly-defined global locomotion states, although a clear active wakefulness state was observed in 4 out of 16 animals 5–6 hr prior to L4leth.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data.

claim: Gradual transitions between directed locomotion and dwelling were commonly observed in crh-1 mutants during the period 5-6 hr prior to L4leth, in contrast to the abrupt wild-type switching.
source: Gradual transitions between directed locomotion and dwelling were commonly observed during this period, in contrast to the abrupt wild-type switching.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: crh-1 mutants exhibited lower overall velocities outside of lethargus.
source: In addition, the mutants exhibited lower overall velocities and increased backward locomotion.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: crh-1 mutants exhibited increased backward locomotion outside of lethargus.
source: In addition, the mutants exhibited lower overall velocities and increased backward locomotion.

claim: During L4leth, the dynamics of quiescence of crh-1 mutants were similar to wild-type.
source: During L4leth, the dynamics of quiescence of crh-1 mutants were similar to wild-type (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: crh-1 mutants showed significantly increased levels of directed (forward and backward) locomotion during motion bouts as compared to wild-type.
source: However, the mutants did show significantly increased levels of directed (forward and backward) locomotion during motion bouts as compared to wild-type (Figures 6 and 8B).
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 8B.

claim: The levels of directed motion during lethargus of crh-1 mutants were similar to those of kin-2 and acy-1(gf) mutants.
source: The levels of directed motion during lethargus of crh-1 mutants were similar to those of kin-2 and acy-1(gf) mutants, possibly indicating a disruption to lethargus behavior.

claim: Two downstream targets of PKA, namely neuropeptide release and CREB, acted coherently to stabilize active wakefulness during L4int.
source: We concluded that two of the downstream targets of PKA, namely neuropeptide release and CREB, acted coherently to stabilize active wakefulness during L4int, while playing a minor role in regulating quiescence and locomotion during lethargus.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of unc-31 and crh-1 mutant experiments.

claim: Neuropeptide release and CREB play a minor role in regulating quiescence and locomotion during lethargus.
source: We concluded that two of the downstream targets of PKA, namely neuropeptide release and CREB, acted coherently to stabilize active wakefulness during L4int, while playing a minor role in regulating quiescence and locomotion during lethargus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that unc-31 and crh-1 mutants show relatively normal behavior during lethargus.

claim: Quiet wakefulness was previously reported in diverse species such as various mammals, birds and reptiles.
source: Quiet wakefulness was previously reported in diverse species such as various mammals, birds and reptiles, and can comprise a large percentage of the waking state (Ruckebusch, 1972; Flanigan, 1973; Campbell and Tobler, 1984).

claim: Quiet wakefulness can comprise a large percentage of the waking state in various species.
source: Quiet wakefulness was previously reported in diverse species such as various mammals, birds and reptiles, and can comprise a large percentage of the waking state (Ruckebusch, 1972; Flanigan, 1973; Campbell and Tobler, 1984).

claim: Quiet wakefulness was not previously reported in nematodes.
source: However, to the best of our knowledge, quiet wakefulness was not previously reported in nematodes.

claim: During larval development, C. elegans is required to integrate newly differentiated neurons into its neural circuits.
source: During its larval development the nematode C. elegans is required to integrate newly differentiated neurons into its neural circuits (Sulston, 1976; Sulston and Horvitz, 1977; White et al., 1986) and to reshape the connections of existing cells (White et al., 1978; Thomas et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: During larval development, C. elegans is required to reshape the connections of existing cells.
source: During its larval development the nematode C. elegans is required to integrate newly differentiated neurons into its neural circuits (Sulston, 1976; Sulston and Horvitz, 1977; White et al., 1986) and to reshape the connections of existing cells (White et al., 1978; Thomas et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 2-4 hr prior to lethargus, the seam cells exhibit increased synthetic activity and begin to deposit the new cuticle.
source: In particular, 2–4 hr prior to lethargus, the seam cells exhibit increased synthetic activity and begin to deposit the new cuticle (Singh and Sulston, 1978; Monsalve et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The timing of quiet wakefulness coincided with the timing of increased seam cell synthetic activity.
source: The timing of quiet wakefulness that we observed coincided with the timing of this activity.
evidence: This is an observation comparing the timing of two phenomena.

claim: Quiet wakefulness may assist with maintaining an appropriate energy balance during cuticle synthesis.
source: Thus, it is possible that this state may assist with maintaining an appropriate energy balance.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the function of quiet wakefulness.

claim: The global locomotion states reported in this study are distinct from the cGMP-dependent short intervals of continuous roaming or dwelling behavior previously described in adults.
source: We note that the global locomotion states that we report are distinct from the cGMP-dependent short intervals of continuous roaming or dwelling behavior, previously described in adults (Fujiwara et al., 2002).
evidence: This distinguishes the current findings from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: Upregulating Gαs signaling stabilized active wakefulness.

evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from kin-2 and acy-1(gf) mutants.

claim: Downregulating Gαs signaling destabilized active wakefulness.
source: We have shown that upregulating or downregulating Gαs signaling stabilized or destabilized active wakefulness respectively.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from acy-1(lf) mutants.

claim: UNC-31 is a gene encoding the calcium-dependent activator protein for secretion (CAPS) required for the priming and docking of DCVs.
source: Downregulated neuropeptide release in unc-31 mutants, a gene encoding the calcium-dependent activator protein for secretion (CAPS) required for the priming and docking of DCVs (Speese et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2010), affected behavior similarly to downregulated Gαs signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PKA catalyzes the phosphorylation of tomosyn, a highly-conserved syntaxin-binding protein.
source: Moreover, PKA was shown to catalyze the phosphorylation of tomosyn, a highly-conserved syntaxin-binding protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PKA function.

claim: Phosphorylation of tomosyn by PKA reduced its interaction with syntaxin and enhanced the formation of the SNARE complex.
source: Phosphorylation of tomosyn by PKA reduced its interaction with syntaxin and enhanced the formation of the SNARE complex (Baba et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baba et al., 2005.

claim: In C. elegans, tomosyn (TOM-1) negatively regulates synaptic transmitter release.
source: In C. elegans, tomosyn (TOM-1) was shown to negatively regulate synaptic transmitter release and UNC-31/CAPS-dependent neuropeptide release (Gracheva et al., 2007a), and KIN-1 alleviated the suppression of both processes by phosphorylating TOM-1 (J Richmond, personal communications, February 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gracheva et al., 2007a.

claim: In C. elegans, tomosyn (TOM-1) negatively regulates UNC-31/CAPS-dependent neuropeptide release.
source: In C. elegans, tomosyn (TOM-1) was shown to negatively regulate synaptic transmitter release and UNC-31/CAPS-dependent neuropeptide release (Gracheva et al., 2007a), and KIN-1 alleviated the suppression of both processes by phosphorylating TOM-1 (J Richmond, personal communications, February 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gracheva et al., 2007a.

claim: KIN-1 alleviated the suppression of synaptic transmitter release and neuropeptide release by phosphorylating TOM-1.
source: In C. elegans, tomosyn (TOM-1) was shown to negatively regulate synaptic transmitter release and UNC-31/CAPS-dependent neuropeptide release (Gracheva et al., 2007a), and KIN-1 alleviated the suppression of both processes by phosphorylating TOM-1 (J Richmond, personal communications, February 2013).
evidence: This is supported by personal communication.

claim: A mutation in the tom-1 gene suppressed behavioral deficits in unc-31 mutants.
source: Interestingly, a mutation in the tom-1 gene suppressed behavioral deficits and DCV accumulation in unc-31 mutants (Gracheva et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gracheva et al., 2007a.

claim: A mutation in the tom-1 gene suppressed DCV accumulation in unc-31 mutants.
source: Interestingly, a mutation in the tom-1 gene suppressed behavioral deficits and DCV accumulation in unc-31 mutants (Gracheva et al., 2007a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gracheva et al., 2007a.

claim: Enhanced PKA activity is sufficient for bypassing the requirement for UNC-31 for the release of DCVs.
source: Similarly, enhanced PKA activity was shown to be sufficient for bypassing the requirement for UNC-31 for the release of DCVs (Zhou et al., 2007; Perez-Mansilla and Nurrish, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2007 and Perez-Mansilla and Nurrish, 2009.

claim: KIN-1 and TOM-1 regulate locomotion.
source: Taken together, these findings support a model in which KIN-1 and TOM-1 regulate locomotion.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined evidence about PKA, tomosyn, and their effects on locomotion.

claim: Upregulating Gαs signaling resulted in enhanced active wakefulness outside of lethargus.
source: Upregulating Gαs signaling resulted in enhanced active wakefulness outside of lethargus and enhanced directed locomotion during L4leth, mirroring previous findings in Drosophila melanogaster and in C. elegans (Joiner et al., 2006; Belfer and Raizen, 2013).
evidence: This is observed from experimental data and consistent with previous findings.

claim: Upregulating Gαs signaling resulted in enhanced directed locomotion during L4leth.
source: Upregulating Gαs signaling resulted in enhanced active wakefulness outside of lethargus and enhanced directed locomotion during L4leth, mirroring previous findings in Drosophila melanogaster and in C. elegans (Joiner et al., 2006; Belfer and Raizen, 2013).
evidence: This is observed from experimental data and consistent with previous findings.

claim: Acute activation of the photoactivated adenylyl cyclase PACα in cholinergic neurons evoked an enhanced activity response.
source: These results were also consistent with a previous observation that acute activation of the photoactivated adenylyl cyclase PACα in cholinergic neurons evoked an enhanced activity response (Weissenberger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weissenberger et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of CREB function resulted in an enhancement of directed locomotion during lethargus.
source: However, loss of CREB function resulted in an enhancement of directed locomotion, as well as changes in the dynamics of bouts of motion and quiescence (Figure 8C,D), during lethargus.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: Loss of CREB function resulted in changes in the dynamics of bouts of motion and quiescence during lethargus.
source: However, loss of CREB function resulted in an enhancement of directed locomotion, as well as changes in the dynamics of bouts of motion and quiescence (Figure 8C,D), during lethargus.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: crh-1 mutants exhibited strong locomotion defects outside of lethargus.
source: In addition, crh-1 mutants exhibited strong locomotion defects outside of lethargus.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Studies of the effects of cAMP signaling on sleep in D. melanogaster and in mice have demonstrated that CREB, when activated by PKA, promotes the duration of wakefulness.
source: Studies of the effects of cAMP signaling on sleep in D. melanogaster and in mice have demonstrated that CREB, when activated by PKA, promotes the duration of wakefulness (Hendricks et al., 2001; Graves et al., 2003; Shaw and Franken, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in other organisms.

claim: Adenylyl cyclase activity increases the intensity of nighttime sleep in Drosophila.
source: Interestingly, a recent study reported that adenylyl cyclase activity increases the intensity of nighttime sleep in Drosophila (van Alphen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Alphen et al., 2013.

claim: Both PKA-dependent pathways (neuropeptide release and CREB) acted in concert to regulate active wakefulness during L4int and the early young adult stages.
source: Taken together, our analyses indicated that both PKA-dependent pathways acted in concert to regulate active wakefulness during L4int and the early young adult stages.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental results of multiple mutants.

claim: The space of shapes adopted by C. elegans is low dimensional.
source: It was recently shown that the space of shapes adopted by the nematode C. elegans is low dimensional, and that these dimensions ('eigenworms') can provide a quantitative description of behavior (Stephens et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stephens et al., 2008.

claim: Eigenworms can provide a quantitative description of C. elegans behavior.
source: It was recently shown that the space of shapes adopted by the nematode C. elegans is low dimensional, and that these dimensions ('eigenworms') can provide a quantitative description of behavior (Stephens et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stephens et al., 2008.

claim: C. elegans does not maintain a 'mental map' of its environment.
source: As in the case of the eigenworms, one underlying assumption of this analysis is that C. elegans does not maintain a 'mental map' of its environment, nor does it keep track of its own acceleration in the laboratory frame of reference.
evidence: This is an assumption underlying the analysis approach.

claim: C. elegans does not keep track of its own acceleration in the laboratory frame of reference.
source: As in the case of the eigenworms, one underlying assumption of this analysis is that C. elegans does not maintain a 'mental map' of its environment, nor does it keep track of its own acceleration in the laboratory frame of reference.
evidence: This is an assumption underlying the analysis approach.

claim: C. elegans responds to external and internal cues solely by altering its own body-posture.
source: Rather, it responds to external and internal cues solely by altering its own body-posture.
evidence: This is an assumption underlying the analysis approach.

claim: The primary task of the motor neurons during directional motion is to generate body-bends and propagate them along the body in the appropriate direction.
source: Specifically, the primary task of the motor neurons during directional motion is to generate body-bends and propagate them along the body in the appropriate direction (Gray et al., 2005; Stetina et al., 2006; Stephens et al., 2008; Haspel and O'Donovan, 2011; Boyle et al., 2011; Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Tracking each body-bend from initiation to eventual demise provides direct experimental measurements of the basic building blocks of nematode locomotion.
source: Tracking each body-bend from initiation to eventual demise thus provides direct experimental measurements of the basic building blocks of nematode locomotion.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the approach used in the study.

claim: Animals were synchronized by restricting the duration of egg-laying to 6 hr.
source: Animals were synchronized by restricting the duration of egg-laying (placing gravid adults on plates for 6 hr, removing the parents, and selecting L4s 3 days later), grown at 20°C on standard NGM plates, and fed OP50 bacteria until their mid L4int larva stage.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: Behavior was recorded for 10 hr at a rate of 10 frames per second.
source: Behavior was recorded for 10 hr at a rate of 10 frames per second using a 5 megapixels CCD camera (Prosilica GC2450, 2448 × 2050 pixels, Allied Vision Technologies, Stadtroda, Germany).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: The rate of segmentation failure was typically 5% of all frames.
source: The rate of segmentation failure, where the animals could not be properly identified, was typically 5% of all frames.
evidence: This describes the performance of the image analysis method.

claim: PyCelegans identifies the body of the animal in each frame and calculates the coordinates of 100 points along its midline, ordered from head to tail.
source: Similar to previously described methods (Husson et al., 2013), PyCelegans identifies the body of the animal in each frame and calculates the coordinates of 100 points along its midline, ordered from head to tail.
evidence: This describes the computational method used.

claim: Each midline was divided into 20 equal segments and the local angle at each of the inner 18 segments was calculated.
source: Each midline was divided into 20 equal segments and the local angle at each of the inner 18 segments was calculated as shown in Figure 1A.
evidence: This describes the computational method used.

claim: Body-bends were defined as positions of local spatial maxima or minima of the angles.
source: Body-bends were defined as positions of local spatial maxima or minima of the angles (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the definition used in the analysis.

claim: Forward locomotion was defined by the propagation of bends in the anterior-posterior direction that persisted for at least three consecutive midline segments.
source: Forward locomotion was defined by the propagation of bends in the anterior-posterior direction that persisted for at least three consecutive midline segments.
evidence: This describes the definition used in the analysis.

claim: Quiescence of an individual segment was defined as an interval in which the rate of change of the corresponding angle did not exceed a threshold of 0.01 radians/sec.
source: Quiescence of an individual segment was defined as an interval in which the rate of change of the corresponding angle did not exceed a threshold of 0.01 radians/sec.
evidence: This describes the definition used in the analysis.

claim: Whole-animal quiescence was defined as the state where the most anterior angle and at least 16 of the remaining 17 angles were quiescent.
source: Whole-animal quiescence was defined as the state where the most anterior angle (between the head and neck segments) and at least 16 of the remaining 17 angles were quiescent.
evidence: This describes the definition used in the analysis.
